title: Standardize the Approval Request Format
scenario: It is 6:35 AM. Today's brief will need a manager sign-off, and past requests have been inconsistent - some named the hub, some forgot the deadline, so approvals dragged. Before the workflow sends anything, write down the one request format every approval will use.
input: The desk agreed on a standard for brief-approval requests. Every request must state the hub, the percent move, the threshold that was crossed, and the response deadline. Requests use the subject format: APPROVAL NEEDED: <hub> <move>% - morning brief. The standard response deadline is 30 minutes. The template is owned by the Risk Desk Lead and changes require sign-off from the Desk Manager. Record this as version 1.0.0.
instructions: Name the template so other steps can refer to it.
Record the subject format exactly as agreed.
Set responseDeadlineMinutes as a plain number.
Record the owner, the approver of changes, and the version.
Validate when every field is filled.
copilotPrompt: Draft a JSON approval-request template with templateName, version, owner, approver, subjectFormat, and responseDeadlineMinutes. Use a plain number for the deadline and record who owns the template and who approves changes.
successMessage: Approval template recorded. The routing step can now generate consistent, governed sign-off requests.

intro.heading: Before you build: governed request formats

sections.title: Why handoffs need templates
sections.body: An approval is a handoff to a human. If every request is written differently, the approver must reconstruct context each time, and requests get slower and less comparable. A template guarantees the same required facts appear every time.

sections.title: Required fields are the standard
sections.body: The desk agreed each request must state the hub, the move, the threshold crossed, and the deadline. Those are not style choices - they are the minimum an approver needs to decide without asking follow-up questions.

sections.title: A deadline is a field, not a hope
sections.body: Putting responseDeadlineMinutes in the template turns 'please respond soon' into a value automation can act on later - for reminders, escalation, or timeout paths.

sections.title: Same governance pattern, second rep
sections.body: Like the Threshold Policy, this template has an owner, an approver of changes, and a version. Governance objects all share that shape - this lesson is your second repetition of it.

intro.jsonExample:
{
  "templateName": "Outage Approval Request",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "owner": "Ops Lead",
  "approver": "Site Manager",
  "subjectFormat": "APPROVAL NEEDED: <site> outage window",
  "responseDeadlineMinutes": 60
}

fieldGuide.meaning: A clear, reusable name for this request format.
fieldGuide.hint: Name it so Approval Route can refer to it.

fieldGuide.meaning: The version so format changes can be tracked.
fieldGuide.hint: The agreement says to record version 1.0.0.

fieldGuide.meaning: Who must sign off on changes to the template.
fieldGuide.hint: The agreement names who approves changes.

fieldGuide.meaning: The standard subject line every request uses.
fieldGuide.hint: Copy the agreed subject format from the input.

fieldGuide.meaning: How long the approver has to respond, in minutes.
fieldGuide.hint: A plain number - no quotes, no 'minutes'.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd write a reusable message template with blanks (merge fields) so every approval request reads the same and just swaps the numbers.

takeaway.heading: Approval template recorded
points: You turned a desk agreement into a named, versioned request format with an owner.
Every future approval request now carries the same required facts: hub, move, threshold, deadline.
The deadline is a machine-readable field, which later enables reminders and timeout handling.
Approval Route reuses this template next - watch for the subject line reappearing there.
The workflow can now create approval requests in a consistent governed format.
